parole.significato: Forms feminine nouns from masculine nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ъка (-ŭka), from Proto-Slavic *-ъka.

parole.significato: Forms nouns that indicate the action or result of a verb
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ѣль (-jělĭ), reanalyzed as plural, from Proto-Slavic *-ělь.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives and nouns indicating origin or place of birth (such as from a certain city or region), or occasionally…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ѣнинъ (-jěninŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ěninъ. Might also be conflated with Latin -iānus.

parole.significato: noun suffix used to denote a place
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ище (-ište), from Proto-Slavic *-išče.

parole.significato: Used to make feminine forms of some masculine nouns, e.g. professions; -ess
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ица (-ica), from Proto-Slavic *-ica.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic адамантъ (adamantŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic агарѣнинъ (agarěninŭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic агода (agoda), from Proto-Slavic *agoda.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic анг҄ельскъ (angʹjelĭskŭ). First attested in 1588.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic архангелъ (arxangelŭ), from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic архидиꙗконъ (arxidijakonŭ), from Ancient Greek ἀρχιδιάκονος (arkhidiákonos). Equivalent to arhi- + diacon.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic архиманьдритъ (arximanĭdritŭ), from Greek αρχιμανδρίτης (archimandrítis).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic азъбоуковьно (azŭbukovĭno), from азъбукꙑ (azŭbuky), from азъ (azŭ) + боукꙑ (buky).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic баснь (basnĭ), from Proto-Slavic *basnь.

parole.testo: From earlier form bezaconie, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безакониѥ (bezakonije), from Proto-Slavic *bez (“without”) + *zakonъ (“law”) + *-ьje (denominal, forming collective nouns).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безъчьстьникъ (bezŭčĭstĭnikŭ), from безъ- (bezŭ-) + чьсть (čĭstĭ) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bez- (“without”) + *čьstь (“honor”) + *-nikъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѣлчоугъ (bělčugŭ), of Turkic origin. Compare Bulgarian белчуг (belčug), Kalmyk билцг (biltsg, “ring”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic без (bez), from Proto-Slavic *bez.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic веззаконику (vezzakoniku).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic беззаконовати (bezzakonovati), from без- (bez-, “without”) + законъ (zakonŭ, “law”) + -овати (-ovati, verb suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безбожьникъ (bezbožĭnikŭ), from без (bez, “without”) + богъ (bogŭ, “god”) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безгласиѥ (bezglasije), from без- (bez-, “without”) + гласъ (glasŭ, “voice”) + -иѥ (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бездъна (bezdŭna), from Proto-Slavic *bezdъna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бичь (bičĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bičь.

parole.significato: ex-, former (preceding a medieval rank in Wallachia or Moldavia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бꙑвъ (byvŭ), from Proto-Slavic *byvъ (“former”), from *byti (“to be”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бꙑволъ (byvolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *byvolъ, from Vulgar Latin *būvalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos). Doublet of bour, which was inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic влаговорецъ (vlagovorecŭ).

parole.significato: kind, gentle, soft, sweet, calm, mild, benign
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блаженъ (blaženŭ, “pleasant”).

parole.significato: soft, shy, silly, dull, weak, foolish, sheepish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благъ (blagŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bolgъ (“good”). Compare Serbo-Croatian blag.

parole.significato: dish, bowl, container or receptacle for food
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блюдо (bljudo), from Proto-Slavic *bľudo.

parole.significato: to speak a foreign tongue that cannot be understood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодарити (blagodariti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бладникъ (bladnikŭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic боиница (boinica).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бодль (bodlĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bodъľь (“needle, pointy tip”). Compare Bulgarian бодил (bodil).

parole.significato: to ail (to be ill; to suffer; to be troubled)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic болѣти (bolěti), from Proto-Slavic *bolěti. By surface analysis, boală + -i.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic больница (bolĭnica), from *bolь (“pain”) + *-nikъ + *-a. Compare Russian больни́ца (bolʹníca).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бебръ (bebrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bebrъ.

parole.significato: ford (location where a stream is shallow)

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic боукъварь (bukŭvarĭ), from боукꙑ (buky, “letter”), from Proto-Slavic *buky. Compare Serbo-Croatian буквар (“primer”), Macedonian буквар (bukvar, “primer”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic боукварь (bukvarĭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic брьвьно (brĭvĭno), from Proto-Slavic *brьvьno.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѣжаниѥ (běžanije, “escape”), from бѣжати (běžati) + -аниѥ (-anije), from Proto-Slavic *běžati (“to flee, to escape”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic калѩнь (kaljęnĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic камилавка (kamilavka).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic камата (kamata), from Ancient Greek κάματος (kámatos). Compare Serbo-Croatian kamata, Macedonian камата (kamata).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic канъдило (kanŭdilo) or Greek καντήλα (kantíla), κάνδηλα (kándila), from Latin candēla. Compare Bulgarian кандило (kandilo), Serbo-Croatian kàndilo, Aromanian cãndilã. Compare also Turkish kandil.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic канонъ (kanonŭ), from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic капище (kapište), from капь (kapĭ, “idol, image”) + -ище (-ište). Compare Serbo-Croatian kapište, Bulgarian капище (kapište), Polish kapiszcze, Russian капище (kapišče).

parole.significato: Katavasia (a type of Eastern Orthodox hymn)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic катавасие (katavasije), from Greek καταβασία (katavasía).

parole.significato: homily, a sermon explaining the gospel
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic казаниѥ (kazanije, “instruction”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic часословець (časoslovecĭ).

parole.significato: group, band, gang, pack, troop, flock
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чета (četa), from Proto-Slavic *četa.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кедръ (kedrŭ), from Greek κέδρος (kédros). Doublet of cedru.

parole.significato: steward in charge of the cellars and supplies
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic келарь (kelarĭ), from Greek κελλάριος (kellários).

parole.significato: Caesar (title of a Roman or Byzantine emperor)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кесарь (kesarĭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic китъ (kitŭ), from Greek κήτος (kítos). Used around the 16th century.

parole.significato: box on the altar in which the communion wafer is kept
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кивотъ (kivotŭ), from Greek κιβώτιον (kivótion), from κῑβωτός (kivotós, “wooden chest”).

parole.significato: high social position in the Middle Ages
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чинъ (činŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чинначиалъникъ (činnačialŭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чьсть (čĭstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷit-tis.

parole.significato: to revere, honor, esteem, respect, pay homage to
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чьстити (čĭstiti), form of чьтити (čĭtiti, “to respect”), from Proto-Slavic *čьstiti.

parole.significato: bone, usually large, with or without meat on it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic члѣнъ (člěnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čelnъ (“member, part”). Compare Bulgarian член (člen, “member, limb”), Serbo-Croatian члан (“member”), Czech člen (“member”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic четврьтъ (četvrĭtŭ, “quarter”), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъ. Compare Bulgarian четвърт (četvărt).

parole.significato: herd, flock, drove (of cattle or other horned animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрѣда (črěda), from Proto-Slavic *čerda (“herd, flock”), from Proto-Indo-European *kerdʰ-. Doublet of cârd and ciurdă. Compare (obsolete) Serbo-Croatian čreda, Russian череда́ (čeredá, “sequence, train”), English herd.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клопотъ (klopotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *klopotъ.

parole.significato: person in charge with supplying the royal court

parole.significato: ruler of a state or principality in past times
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кънѧзь (kŭnęzĭ, “prince”), from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь (“prince”), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz. The latter sense was influenced by Russian князь (knjazʹ) and Ukrainian князь (knjazʹ). Doublet of chinez.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣсѣка (prěsěka), from прѣсѣкати (prěsěkati).

parole.significato: saddle, ridge (a ridge connecting two summits)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣслопъ (prěslopŭ). Cognate with Bulgarian преслоп (preslop).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пристанище (pristanište).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приставъ (pristavŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приставьникъ (pristavĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстолъ (prěstolŭ), from прѣ- (prě-) + столъ (stolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stolъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пристѫпити (pristǫpiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣставити (prěstaviti), from прѣ- (prě-) + ставити (staviti), from Proto-Slavic *staviti.

parole.significato: to look, gaze, regard, watch, behold
parole.testo: From older form prăvi, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic правити (praviti), from Proto-Slavic *praviti (“to twist, to turn”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣзьрѣти (prězĭrěti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пришьльць (prišĭlĭcĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прообразити (proobraziti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прообразовати (proobrazovati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прокажениѥ (prokaženije).

parole.significato: a clerk in the princely court of Wallachia and Moldavia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прочелникъ (pročelnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прочии (pročii). Compare Russian прочий (pročij, “other”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic продоухъ (produxŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъградиѥ (podŭgradije, “suburb”), from подъ (podŭ, “under”) + градъ (gradŭ, “city”), from Proto-Slavic *podъ + *gordъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проводъ (provodŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проводити (provoditi).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic произволѥниѥ (proizvoljenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic промишлѥниѥ (promišljenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проповѣданиѥ (propovědanije).

parole.significato: to teach, to spread ideas or religious doctrines
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проповѣдати (propovědati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проповѣдьникъ (propovědĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, propovedi + -nic.

parole.significato: to teach, to spread ideas or religious doctrines
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проповѣдати (propovědati), from повѣдѣти (pověděti, “deliver a sermon”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подъпрѣти (podŭprěti), from подъ- (podŭ-) + прѣти (prěti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пророкъ (prorokŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пророчьствиѥ (proročĭstvije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пророчица (proročica).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проскомидиꙗ (proskomidija), from Byzantine Greek Προσκομιδή (Proskomidḗ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прославити (proslaviti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic простъ (prostŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prostъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic простити (prostiti, “to forgive”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic протопопъ (protopopŭ), from Koine Greek πρωτοπαπάς (prōtopapás).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic провидець (providecĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic процѣпъ (procěpŭ). Compare Bulgarian процеп (procep).

parole.significato: sand or gravel found on the bottom of bodies of water or within the Earth's crust
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѫдъ (prǫdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prǫdъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прьстъ (prĭstŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьrstъ (“finger”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прьстень (prĭstenĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьrsty.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прꙑснѫти (prysnǫti). First attested in 1683.

parole.significato: to fry (to cook in hot fat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пражити (pražiti), from Proto-Slavic *pražiti. Compare Ukrainian пряжити (prjažyty), Serbo-Croatian pražiti.

parole.significato: to live in a certain place
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣмоудити (prěmuditi).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пропасть (propastĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прасити (prasiti), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *porsę (“piglet”). Compare Bulgarian прася (prasja).

parole.significato: to knock down, throw down, overthrow
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic провалити (provaliti), from про- (pro-) + валити (valiti), from Proto-Slavic *valiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian provaliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic привилиѥ (privilije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьновати (prazdĭnovati), from праздьнъ (prazdĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прашити (prašiti), from Proto-Slavic *poršiti, compare with praf. Compare also Aromanian prãshescu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic псалъмъ (psalŭmŭ), from Byzantine Greek ψαλμός (psalmós).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic псалътꙑр҄ь (psalŭtyrʹĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic повонь (povonĭ), from по- (po-) + вода (voda, “water”) + -ьнь (-ĭnĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поустꙑни (pustyni), from Proto-Slavic *pustyni, from *pustъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поустиньникъ (pustinĭnikŭ), from поустꙑни (pustyni, “wilderness”) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pustyni (“wilderness”), from *pustъ (“empty”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поздериѥ (pozderije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пькълъ (pĭkŭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьkъlъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пыха (pyxa).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плъниѥ (plŭnije, “flow, stream”), from Proto-Slavic *pъlniti (“to fill”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пѫдарь (pǫdarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi (“to chase”).

parole.significato: to watch, lurk, wait for, lie in wait, lie in ambush, spy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пѫдити (pǫditi), from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пръгавъ (prŭgavŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пръга (prŭga), from Proto-Slavic *pьrga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прътъ (prŭtŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пръводиꙗконъ (prŭvodijakonŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пръвосѣдѣниѥ (prŭvosěděnije), from сѣдѣти (sěděti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пьрѣти (pĭrěti), from Proto-Slavic *pьrěti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плъхъ (plŭxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pьlxъ, possibly from Proto-Balto-Slavic *peliā, from Proto-Indo-European *pelH-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плъсть (plŭstĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *паѭжина (*pajǫžina), from паѫкъ (paǫkŭ) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ. Compare Aromanian pangu, Bulgarian паяжина (pajažina).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic палити (paliti), from Proto-Slavic *paliti. Compare Serbo-Croatian paliti. Also found in Aromanian as pãlescu, probably indicating an early borrowing.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *пометоухъ (*pometuxŭ), from пометати (pometati, “to sweep”), from метати (metati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пъприще (pŭprište), поприще (poprište).

parole.significato: to guard, watch over, take care of, protect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пазити (paziti), from Proto-Slavic *paziti. Compare Aromanian pãzescu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ракъ (rakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rakъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian rak, Czech rak, Polish rak.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рай (raj), from Proto-Slavic *rajь, borrowed from Iranian, from Proto-Iranian *raHíš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *raHíš, from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рамьнъ (ramĭnŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рана (rana), from Proto-Slavic *rana. Compare Serbo-Croatian rana, Bulgarian рана (rana), Russian рана (rana). cf. also Aromanian aranã, ranã.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic растъ (rastŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разьно (razĭno).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic робъ (robŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”). Doublet of orb, which was inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic работа (rabota), from Proto-Slavic *orbota. Doublet of robot.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родъ (rodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родити (roditi), from Proto-Slavic *roditi.

parole.significato: sedge (Carex), greater pond sedge (Carex riparia) or true fox-sedge (Carex vulpina)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рогоз (rogoz), from Proto-Slavic *rogozъ. Compare also Aromanian arugoz.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рои (roi), from Proto-Slavic *rojь. Compare Czech roj, Slovak roj and Serbo-Croatian roj.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рожденикъ (roždenikŭ).

parole.significato: Eastern Orthodox decoration on the arm of the priest's clothes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рȢкавица (rȢkavica).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родъ (rodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ.

parole.significato: laundry (that which needs to be, is, or has been laundered)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роухо (ruxo), from Proto-Slavic *ruxo. Compare Bulgarian рухо (ruho), Serbo-Croatian ruho.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роумѣнъ (ruměnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ruměnъ (“ruddy”). Compare Bulgarian румен (rumen), Serbo-Croatian rumen.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роусъ (rusŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rusъ. Compare Aromanian arus.

parole.significato: rusalka; a Slavic female water spirit associated with death by drowning
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роусалка (rusalka), from Old Church Slavonic роусалиѩ (rusaliję), from Byzantine Greek ῥουσάλια (rhousália), from Latin rōsālia (“festival of the roses”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic роусалиѩ (rusaliję), from Byzantine Greek ρουσάλια (rousália), from Latin rosalia.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic римлꙗнинъ (rimljaninŭ, “Roman”), from Римъ (Rimŭ, “Rome”) (see Râm).

parole.significato: having one testicle (after being castrated poorly)
parole.testo: From râncă (from Old Church Slavonic рѫка (rǫka, “hand”)) + -aci. Other theories are unlikely, such as a Vulgar Latin *rēnicus, from Latin ren (“kidney”) (cf. Spanish rengo), German Ranke (“penis”), or Latin rāmex (“hernia”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рѧдъ (rędŭ, “row, line”), from Proto-Slavic *rędъ. Compare also Albanian rend.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рꙑсь (rysĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rysь. A widely perpetrated false etymology links it to its homonym, claiming that the animal is named for the laughter-like vocalisations.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рътъ (rŭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъtъ. Compare Bulgarian рът (răt) and Russian рот (rot).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рьвьновати (rĭvĭnovati, “to strive after, to envy”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рыкнѫти (ryknǫti). Compare Serbo-Croatian riknuti, Russian рычать (ryčatʹ, “to growl”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рѫкодѣлиѥ (rǫkodělije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рогачь (rogačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rogačь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ранити (raniti, “to wound”), from Proto-Slavic *raniti, from *rana (“wound”). Compare Aromanian arãnescu, arãniri.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ръпътати (rŭpŭtati).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раз- (raz-), from Proto-Slavic *orz-, with some cases possibly based on Latin re- + ex-; compare Old French res- and its modern reflex, ré-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic расколити (raskoliti), from рас- (ras-) + колити (koliti), from *koliti. Compare Serbo-Croatian raskoliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic распетиѥ (raspetije).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic распѫдити (raspǫditi, “to scatter”), from рас- (ras-) + пѫдити (pǫditi), from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *reexpandīre (compare French répandre (“to spread, scatter”)), from expandere.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic распѫтиѥ (raspǫtije), from Proto-Slavic *orzpǫtьje. Compare Russian распутье (rasputʹje).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic растѧгнѫти (rastęgnǫti), from рас- (ras-) + тѧгнѫти (tęgnǫti), from Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic растѫпъ (rastǫpŭ), under the influence of timp.

parole.significato: to divert the flow of a river to catch fish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic расточити (rastočiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic растварꙗти (rastvarjati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic расѫждати (rasǫždati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развити (razviti), from Proto-Slavic *orzbiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian razbiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разбои (razboi), from Proto-Slavic *orzbojь. Compare Serbo-Croatian razboj (“warfare, combat”), Russian разбой (razboj, “robbery”). Cf. also Aromanian arãzboi.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разбоиникъ (razboinikŭ, “robber”), from Proto-Slavic *orzbojьnikъ. Compare Bulgarian разбойник (razbojnik), Serbo-Croatian razbojnik (“outlaw, bandit”), Russian разбойник (razbojnik, “highwayman, robber”). By surface analysis, război + -nic.

parole.significato: to get sick, to fall ill
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разболѣти (razbolěti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раздроушити (razdrušiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развала (razvala).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развѣщати (razvěštati), from раз- (raz-) + вѣщати (věštati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развратити (razvratiti, “to deviate from the path”), from раз- (raz-, “change”) + вратити (vratiti, “to turn”), from Proto-Slavic *vortiti (“to turn”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic садъ (sadŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic самодръжавьнъ (samodrŭžavĭnŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic самогласьнъ (samoglasĭnŭ).

parole.significato: plants sprouted without being purposely planted, from the seeds falling on the ground at harvest
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic самораслъ (samoraslŭ), from Proto-Slavic *samoorstlъ, from *samъ (“self”) + *orsti (“to grow”). Compare Serbo-Croatian samorast.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сатана (satana).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скопєць (skopecĭ) or Russian скопец (skopec).

parole.significato: a youngling of a wild beast
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скимън (skimŭn).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скимьникъ (skimĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, schimă + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скиниꙗ (skinija).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скипътръ (skipŭtrŭ). Doublet of sceptru.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скитъ (skitŭ), from Ancient Greek σκήτη (skḗtē).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скоба (skoba), from Proto-Slavic *skoba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *скокъ (*skokŭ). Compare Bulgarian скок (skok) or Serbo-Croatian skok.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съконьчаниѥ (sŭkonĭčanije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скопити (skopiti), from Proto-Slavic *skopiti (“to castrate”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скоръпии (skorŭpii), from Byzantine Greek σκορπίον (skorpíon). Doublet of scorpion.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скотина (skotina).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сковрада (skovrada), from Proto-Slavic *skovorda (“frying pan”). Compare Russian сковорода (skovoroda).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скрижаль (skrižalĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скробъ (skrobŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скѫпъ (skǫpŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skǫpъ (compare Serbo-Croatian skȗp, Slovene skôp, Bulgarian скъп (skăp)). Compare Aromanian scumpu.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скѫдъ (skǫdŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skǫdьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скръбь (skrŭbĭ, “grief, sorrow”), from Proto-Slavic *skъrbь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврънавъ (skvrŭnavŭ, “polluted, unclean, impure”), from сквръна (skvrŭna, “dirt, filth”) + -авъ (-avŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skvьrna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьна (skvrĭna), from Proto-Slavic *skvьrna. Cognates include Bulgarian скверен (skveren), Russian скверна (skverna), Megleno-Romanian scrămă.

parole.significato: a kind of a religious hymn
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѣдѣло (sědělo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѣдѣльна (sědělĭna).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic септѧбр҄ь (septębrʹĭ), from Byzantine Greek Σεπτέμβριος (Septémbrios), from Latin (mensis) September.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic серафимъ (serafimŭ), from Koine Greek σεραφείμ (serapheím), from Biblical Hebrew שְׂרָפִים (śərāp̄îm), the plural form of שָׂרָף (śārāp̄, “burning one”).
From Old Church Slavonic съвадьникъ (sŭvadĭnikŭ), from съвада (sŭvada) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, sfadă + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвада (sŭvada, “quarrel”), from Proto-Slavic *svarъ (“quarrel, strife”).

parole.significato: a strong smell or smoke resulting from burning meat or fat, or a wax candle, etc., or any strong, heavy smoke or odor
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сквара (skvara), from Proto-Slavic *skvara.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтъ (sŭvětŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъvětъ. The variant sveat is the most conservative from which all other variants derive. Compare Serbo-Croatian savet. Doublet of soviet.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свеклъ (sveklŭ), from Byzantine Greek, from Ancient Greek σεῦκλον (seûklon). Compare Serbo-Croatian cvikla, Bulgarian цвекло (cveklo), Russian свёкла (svjókla); cf. also Hungarian cékla.
From older șfert, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic четврьтъ (četvrĭtŭ), from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian četvrt, Ukrainian чверть (čvertʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic [Term?].
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѣтити (světiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѣтильна (světilĭna).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic светитель (svetitelĭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѣщьникъ (svěštĭnikŭ). Compare Russian свечник (svečnik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѧщениѥ (svęštenije).

parole.significato: to be shy, to be intimidated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѣнити (svěniti), from Proto-Slavic *svěniti (“be shy”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свиниꙗ (svinija).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свита (svita).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвора (sŭvora). Compare also Greek σφόρα (sfóra).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвадити (sŭvaditi). By surface analysis, sfadă + -i.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сикаминиѥ (sikaminije), from Greek συκάμινος (sykáminos).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съхль (sŭxlĭ, “brushwood”), from Proto-Slavic *sъxlь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic силити (siliti), from Proto-Slavic *sila (“force”).

parole.significato: abandoned village, place where a village existed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic селище (selište), from Proto-Slavic *selište, from Proto-Slavic *selo (“village”) + Proto-Slavic *-ište (“place of”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сильнъ (silĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *silьnъ (“strong”), from *sila (“strength”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic силовати (silovati), from Proto-Slavic *silovati, from *sila (“force”). Compare Serbo-Croatian silovati (“to force, to rape”).

parole.significato: disgust, loathing, abhorrence, hatred, aversion, antipathy, revulsion, dislike, ill-will, (deep) grudge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сила (sila), from Proto-Slavic *sila (“force, power, strength”). Compare Aromanian silã, Bulgarian сила (sila), Serbo-Croatian sila.
From Old Church Slavonic сꙑнъ (synŭ), from Proto-Slavic *synъ (“son”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫдиꙗ (sǫdija).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сирѣчь (sirěčĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сириꙗнинъ (sirijaninŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сито (sito), from Proto-Slavic *sito. Compare Bulgarian сито (sito), Serbo-Croatian sito, Polish sito, Aromanian sitã, Albanian sitë.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слабъ (slabŭ), from Proto-Slavic *slàbъ. Compare Aromanian slab, Bulgarian and Macedonian слаб (slab), Serbo-Croatian slȁb.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слатина (slatina), from Proto-Slavic *soltina (“salt marsh”), from *solь (“salt”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic славословити (slavosloviti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic славословиѥ (slavoslovije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слава (slava), from Proto-Slavic *slava.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слѣдити (slěditi).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сълиꙗти (sŭlijati), from Proto-Slavic *sъlijati, from *lijati (“to pour”), from *liti (“to pour”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свободь (svobodĭ), from Proto-Slavic *svoboda (“freedom”). Compare Bulgarian свободен (svoboden).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic своводьникъ (svovodĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, slobod + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic словѣнинъ (slověninŭ). Doublet of sloven. Cf. also șcheau and slav.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic словѣньскъ (slověnĭskŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic словесьнъ (slovesĭnŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слово (slovo), from Proto-Slavic *slovo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоуга (sluga), from Proto-Slavic *sluga. Compare Serbo-Croatian sluga.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоужьба (služĭba), from Proto-Slavic *služьba. Compare Serbo-Croatian služba.

parole.significato: to officiate, perform the functions of some office
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоужити (služiti), from Proto-Slavic *služiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian služiti, Czech sloužit.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слоужьникъ (služĭnikŭ).
From slujnic + -ă, from Old Church Slavonic слоужьникъ (služĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *služьnikъ, from *služiti (“to serve”).

parole.significato: to grow thin, slim, lose weight
parole.testo: From slab + -i, or borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слабити (slabiti). Compare Aromanian slãghescu, slãghiri.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сланина (slanina), from Proto-Slavic *solnina, from *solnъ (“salt”) + *-ina. Compare Bulgarian сланина (slanina), Serbo-Croatian slanina.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic славити (slaviti, “to praise, to glorify”), from Proto-Slavic *slaviti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смѣдъ (smědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *smědъ (“brown”). Compare Serbo-Croatian smeđ, Czech snědý.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѣрѥниѥ (sŭměrjenije).

parole.significato: to be humble, submissive or respectful
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѣрити (sŭměriti), from съ- (sŭ-) + мѣрити (měriti, “to measure”), from Proto-Slavic *měriti (“to measure”), from *měra (“measure”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѣрьнъ (sŭměrĭnŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѣрьникъ (sŭměrĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, smeri + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѧсти (sŭmęsti), from съ- (sŭ-) + мѧсти (męsti), from Proto-Slavic *męsti (“stir, trouble”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смиръна (smirŭna), from Ancient Greek σμύρνα (smúrna).

parole.significato: pitch (dark, extremely viscous material made by distilling tar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смола (smola), from Proto-Slavic *smola.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смокъвинъ (smokŭvinŭ), from смокꙑ (smoky), from Proto-Slavic *smoky, perhaps from Gothic 𐍃𐌼𐌰𐌺𐌺𐌰 (smakka). Compare Bulgarian смокиня (smokinja), Serbo-Croatian smokva.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смрадъ (smradŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смръдѣти (smrŭděti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смучити (smučiti, “to crawl”), from Proto-Slavic *smučati. Cognates include Slovene smučati (“to ski”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съметана (sŭmetana), from Proto-Slavic *sъmetana; possibly an early borrowing to explain for the vowel sound change before nasals. The "n" can be explained by the influence of *sъmęsti. Compare Bulgarian сметана (smetana), Russian сметана (smetana).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смръкъ (smrŭkŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смръкати (smrŭkati), from Proto-Slavic *smъrkati. Compare Czech smrkat, Polish smarkać, Russian сморкать (smorkatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смрадъ (smradŭ, “stench”), from Proto-Slavic *smьrdъ, from *smьrděti (“to stink”). Compare, Serbo-Croatian smrad, Czech smrad.
From earlier iznoavă, from Old Church Slavonic изъ нова (izŭ nova, “again”), from Proto-Slavic *jьz *novъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic снопъ (snopŭ), from Proto-Slavic *snopъ.
Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic съборъ (sŭborŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъborъ (“meeting, gathering”). Doublet of zbor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съборьнъ (sŭborĭnŭ). By surface analysis, sobor + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic согласьна (soglasĭna).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic согласовати (soglasovati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуходолъ (suxodolŭ), from соухъ (suxŭ, “dry”) + долъ (dolŭ, “valley”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сомъ (somŭ), from Proto-Slavic *somъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сърокъ (sŭrokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъrokъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпоити (sŭpoiti, “to bond”), from съ- (sŭ-) + поити (poiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sporъ.
From spor, from Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sporъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исповѣданьѥ (ispovědanĭje).

parole.significato: to confess (unburden oneself of sins in presence of a priest, in order to receive absolution)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исповѣдати (ispovědati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпрѧженъ (sŭpręženŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпрѧтьнъ (sŭprętĭnŭ). Compare Serbo-Croatian spretan, Slovene spreten, Bulgarian спретен (spreten).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпасениѥ (sŭpasenije), from Proto-Slavic *sъpasenьje. Cognates include Serbo-Croatian spasenje.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпасти (sŭpasti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стамьна (stamĭna).

parole.significato: shady place where cattle rest during the midday heat
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic станище (stanište), from станъ (stanŭ) + -ище (-ište), from Proto-Slavic *stanъ (“camp”). Compare Serbo-Croatian stanište.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стѣна (stěna), from Proto-Slavic *stěna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic старьць (starĭcĭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic старость (starostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *starostь (“old age”), from *starъ (“old”). Compare Russian староста (starosta, “bailiff, village elder, churchwarden”), Polish starosta (“leader”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ставило (stavilo), from ставити (staviti) + -ило (-ilo), from Proto-Slavic *staviti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стѣгъ (stěgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stěgъ. Compare Ukrainian стяг (stjah) or Russian стяг (stjag).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стьбль (stĭblĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic степень (stepenĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стькло (stĭklo), from Proto-Slavic *stьklo, from Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌹𐌺𐌻𐍃 (stikls).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стидливъ (stidlivŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътъкнѫти (sŭtŭknǫti), from съ- (sŭ-) + тъкнѫти (tŭknǫti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стихъ (stixŭ), from Ancient Greek στῐ́χος (stĭ́khos, “verse, line of poetry”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стѵхиꙗ (stüxija, “element”).

parole.significato: sticheron, hymn sang in the morning
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стихира (stixira), from Ancient Greek στιχηρον (stikhēron).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стиховьно (stixovĭno).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стогъ (stogŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stogъ.

parole.significato: in medieval Wallachia and Moldavia, the steward of the cooks and gardeners
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стольникъ (stolĭnikŭ), from Old Church Slavonic столъ (stolŭ, “table”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стражьникъ (stražĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, strajă + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стража (straža), from Proto-Slavic *storža. Compare Serbo-Croatian straža.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страньникъ (stranĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страна (strana, “side”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страсть (strastĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стратокамилъ (stratokamilŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страторникъ (stratornikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страшьнъ (strašĭnŭ, “terrible, horrible, feared”), from Proto-Slavic *strašьnъ (“terrible, frightening”), from *straxъ (“terror, fear”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стрѣшина (strěšina), from стрѣха (strěxa) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *strěxa (“roof”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сърѣтениѥ (sŭrětenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътрывати (sŭtryvati), from съ- (sŭ-) + трывати (tryvati), from Proto-Slavic *tryvati (“to scrub”), from *tryti (“to rub”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сърѧща (sŭręšta).
Probably from Old Church Slavonic съкропити (sŭkropiti), from съ- (sŭ-) + кропити (kropiti, “to sprinkle”), from Proto-Slavic *kropiti. Compare Ukrainian скропити (skropyty, “to sprinkle”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стршити (stršiti).

parole.significato: to take out unuseful parts of something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic строужити (stružiti).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic строугъ (strugŭ), from Proto-Slavic *strugъ. Compare Bulgarian струг (strug), Serbo-Croatian strug, Polish strug, Russian струг (strug). The nasal infix may be due to the influence of Greek.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic строуна (struna), from Proto-Slavic *struna (“string”). Cognates include Bulgarian струна (struna), Russian струна (struna), Serbo-Croatian струна, Czech struna, Polish struna, Slovak struna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страданиѥ (stradanije), from Proto-Slavic *stradanьje. Compare Bulgarian страдание (stradanie), Russian страдание (stradanije), Serbo-Croatian stradanje.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страдати (stradati), from Proto-Slavic *stradati (“to suffer”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страстовати (strastovati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътлѣщи (sŭtlěšti, “to crush”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стлъпъ (stlŭpŭ, “pillar, column, tower”), from Proto-Slavic *stъlpъ, alternative form of *stъlbъ. Compare Russian столп (stolp).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стлъпьникъ (stlŭpĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, stâlp + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стрькъ (strĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stьrkъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian štȓk, Macedonian штрк (štrk), Bulgarian щъ́ркел (štắrkel), Aromanian stircu, also Albanian shtërg.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стръвь (strŭvĭ), from a Germanic language, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sterbaną.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ставити (staviti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соукати (sukati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соулица (sulica), from Proto-Slavic *sudlica.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свинець (svinecĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съблазнь (sŭblaznĭ, “temptation”), from съ- (sŭ-) + блазнь (blaznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *blaznь (“bait”).

parole.significato: to fall into sin, to morally decay
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съблазнити (sŭblazniti). Attested in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic садити (saditi), from Proto-Slavic *saditi (“to plant”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмыслити (sŭmysliti).

parole.significato: a mass or prayer for the dead (or also for the sick), done for forty days
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сарандаръ (sarandarŭ), from Greek σαράνταρι (sarántari), from σαράντα (saránta, “forty”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic саракинъ (sarakinŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic саракоусти (sarakusti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сиротъкъ (sirotŭkŭ), from сирота (sirota, “orphan”) + -ъкъ (-ŭkŭ). Compare sărac, from the same root.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съставъ (sŭstavŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътьник (sŭtĭnik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвръщение (sŭvrŭštenije).
Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic съврьшити (sŭvrĭšiti), from съ- (sŭ-) + връшити (vrŭšiti). Compare Serbo-Croatian svršiti / свршити, Russian совершить (soveršitʹ). Doublet of sfârși.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съзьданьѥ (sŭzĭdanĭje).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic таинъ (tainŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tajьnъ. By surface analysis, taină + -ic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic таина (taina), from Proto-Slavic *tajьna. Compare Bulgarian тайна (tajna), Czech tajemství, Polish tajemnica, Russian тайна (tajna), Serbo-Croatian tajna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic талантъ (talantŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тарътаръ (tarŭtarŭ), from Ancient Greek Τάρταρος (Tártaros). Doublet of Tartar.
From tartar (“hell”), from Old Church Slavonic тарътаръ (tarŭtarŭ), from Ancient Greek Τάρταρος (Tártaros).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѣскъ (těskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *těskъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic телѣга (telěga), from Proto-Slavic *telěga. Cognates include Russian телега (telega), Czech taliha, Serbo-Croatian таљиге.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic темель (temelĭ), from Byzantine Greek θεμέλιον (themélion), from Ancient Greek θεμέλιος (themélios). Doublet of temelie. Compare Serbo-Croatian temelj.

parole.significato: foundation (the lowest part of a building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic темелиѥ (temelije), from темель (temelĭ) + -иѥ (-ije), from Byzantine Greek θεμέλιον (themélion), from Ancient Greek θεμέλιος (themélios). Compare Old Serbo-Croatian temelije.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тьмьница (tĭmĭnica), from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnica, from *tьmьnъ + *-ica, from *tьma + *-ьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *timāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic теплота (teplota).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *тѣсковина (*těskovina), from тѣскъ (těskŭ) + -овъ (-ovŭ) + -ина (-ina), from Proto-Slavic *těskъ.

parole.significato: to press grapes or other fruits to make juice or wine
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѣсковати (těskovati), from тѣскъ (těskŭ, “press”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тесла (tesla), from Proto-Slavic *tesla.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тетраевангелиѥ (tetrajevangelije). By surface analysis, tetra- + evanghelie.

parole.significato: to cut obliquely a piece of wood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тесати (tesati), from Proto-Slavic *tesati (“to hew”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тихнѫти (tixnǫti), from тихъ (tixŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tixъ (“quiet”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тина (tina), from Proto-Slavic *tina, cognate with Bulgarian тиня (tinja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тиса (tisa), from Proto-Slavic *tisa.

parole.significato: to blunt, dull, wear down, grind away at
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic точити (točiti), from Proto-Slavic *točiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тъкъма (tŭkŭma). Compare Bulgarian тъкмо (tăkmo), Serbo-Croatian tek, also Russian только (tolʹko).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тъкъмити (tŭkŭmiti), from Proto-Slavic *tъkъmiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian takmiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тоꙗгъ (tojagŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топити (topiti), from Proto-Slavic *topiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian topiti, Bulgarian топя (topja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топлица (toplica), from топлъ (toplŭ) + -ица (-ica), from Proto-Slavic *toplъ (“warm”) + *-ica (“deadjectival suffix”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топоръ (toporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *toporъ, from an Iranian language. Also found in Aromanian as tãpor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic топорище (toporište), from Proto-Slavic *toporište, from *toporъ (“axe”) + *-ište.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трапеза (trapeza), from Ancient Greek τράπεζα (trápeza).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣба (trěba), from Proto-Slavic *terba. Compare Bulgarian трябва (trjabva), Serbo-Croatian treba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣскъ (trěskŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣзвъ (trězvŭ), from Proto-Slavic *terzvъ (“sober”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣбьникъ (trěbĭnikŭ), from трѣба (trěba) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *terba.

parole.significato: to be necessary, to need to, to have to
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣбовати (trěbovati), from Proto-Slavic root *terb- (see *terba).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трьклѧтъ (trĭklętŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трепетьникъ (trepetĭnikŭ), from трепетъ (trepetŭ) + -ьникъ (-ĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тръстиѥ (trŭstije, “reed”), from Proto-Slavic *trъstьje, from *trъstь.

parole.significato: third (preceding a medieval rank in Wallachia or Moldavia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic третии (tretii), from Proto-Slavic *tretь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣзвити (trězviti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трьокаꙗнъ (trĭokajanŭ).

parole.significato: feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic три (tri, “three”) + свѧтитель (svętitelĭ, “saint”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троꙗнъ (trojanŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троица (troica).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тропарь (troparĭ), from Ancient Greek τροπάριον (tropárion).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троскотъ (troskotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *torskotъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣснѫти (trěsnǫti, “to bang, to hit, to strike”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троудити (truditi), from Proto-Slavic *truditi, from *trudъ (“labour”) + *-iti (denominal suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троудьнъ (trudĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trudьnъ, from *trudъ (“labour, effort”) + *-ьnъ. By surface analysis, trudă + -nic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троудъ (trudŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trudъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троупъ (trupŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trupъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѫбица (trǫbica), diminutive of трѫба (trǫba), from Proto-Slavic *trǫba. Doublet of Turbuța.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѫба (trǫba).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѫдавъ (trǫdavŭ), from трѫдъ (trǫdŭ, “illness”) + -авъ (-avŭ). Compare Serbo-Croatian truntav.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѫтити (trǫtiti), from Proto-Slavic *trǫtiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣснѫти (trěsnǫti). Compare Serbo-Croatian tresnuti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тоулити (tuliti), with senses from затулити (zatuliti, “to hide”), from Proto-Slavic *tuliti. Compare Bulgarian туля (tulja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic творениѥ (tvorenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic творець (tvorecĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъкъ (tlŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ. Compare Slovak tĺk.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъкованиѥ (tlŭkovanije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъковьникъ (tlŭkovĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъковати (tlŭkovati, “to explain, to interpret”), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkovati, from *tъlkъ (“interpretation”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫпъ (tǫpŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tǫpъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫпанъ (tǫpanŭ), from Byzantine Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon). Doublet of timpan.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫгъ (tǫgŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫговати (tǫgovati), from тѫга (tǫga), from Proto-Slavic *tǫga (“sadness”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫга (tǫga).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѫжити (tǫžiti), from тѫга (tǫga, “sadness, melancholy”), from Proto-Slavic *tǫga. Not related to tânjală.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тръговище (trŭgovište).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трънъ (trŭnŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic троносаниѥ (tronosanije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic търпѣниѥ (tŭrpěnije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трьти (trĭti), from Proto-Slavic *terti. Compare Serbo-Croatian trti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъмачь (tlŭmačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь (“interpreter”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тлъмачити (tlŭmačiti), from Proto-Slavic *tъlmačiti.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic воѥвода (vojevoda), from Proto-Slavic *vojevoda.

parole.significato: hale, healthy, sturdy, robust, vigorous, stout

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вольнъ (volĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *volьnъ, from *volъ (“sufficiency”) + *-ьnъ (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вапьсати (vapĭsati) or Bulgarian вапсам (vapsam).

parole.significato: official in charge with justice and internal affairs in the Principality of Moldavia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дворьникъ (dvorĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dvorьnikъ, from *dvorъ (“court”) + *-nikъ. Compare Russian дворник (dvornik), Slovak nádvorník, Hungarian nádor.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въскръсениѥ (vŭskrŭsenije). First attested in 1741.

parole.significato: in Orthodox liturgy, a part of a prayer that is uttered aloud and clearly
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възгласъ (vŭzglasŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възглашениѥ (vŭzglašenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врабии (vrabii), from Proto-Slavic *vorbь. Compare Serbo-Croatian vrabac, Russian воробе́й (vorobéj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдьнъ (vrědĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *verdьnъ.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic влъшьвьникъ (vlŭšĭvĭnikŭ).
From vânj + -os, from Old Church Slavonic вѫзъ (vǫzŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vǫzъ.

parole.significato: to thrust, poke or shove into

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic весло (veslo), from Proto-Slavic *veslo.

parole.significato: to show clearly, bring to light, make clear or apparent, indicate, betoken, bewray
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вадити (vaditi), from Proto-Slavic *vaditi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсприемьникъ (vŭsprijemĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въздоухъ (vŭzduxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъzduxъ. Compare Russian воздух (vozdux).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въздръжьникъ (vŭzdrŭžĭnikŭ).

parole.significato: feast of exaltation of the Holy Cross

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зачало (začalo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зачетиѥ (začetije).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съгръчити (sŭgrŭčiti).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зѫбьць (zǫbĭcĭ), from зѫбъ (zǫbŭ, “tooth”) + -ьць (-ĭcĭ). Compare Bulgarian зъбец (zăbec).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злоба (zloba).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злочестивъ (zločestivŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злославиѥ (zloslavije).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic завора (zavora, “lock”).

From în- + Old Church Slavonic дрьзнѫти (drĭznǫti), from Proto-Slavic *dьrznǫti.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шестаръ (šestarŭ).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кожа (koža), or from a (South) Slavic koža, from Proto-Slavic *koža. Compare Serbo-Croatian ко̏жа, Bulgarian кожа (koža). Compare also Aromanian coaji.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic опинъка (opinŭka). Compare Bulgarian опинка (opinka). Probably ultimately from Albanian opingë, either directly or via Old Church Slavonic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пизарь (pizarĭ) (however, the normal result would have been *pisare) or from Polish pisarz, from Old Church Slavonic пьсати (pĭsati, “to write”).
